Hello!

This is a topic that has often been on mind since getting engaged as I find myself amidst my single friends who always seem to share repetitive stories of frustration and failed relationships. It's easy to blame the other person (as my friends tend to do), assuming "he just wasn't for me" or "we couldn't see eye to eye on too many things", all of which may have been true but so typically aren't the only factors that break the bond. The way I see it, many of us are too proud to admit our own shortcomings, especially when it comes to overlooking some of the negatives in order to correctly reward our partners for all the positive things they do in our lives.

While some behaviors and feelings come naturally in a relationship, other things involve a bit of communication, practice, and a whole lot of patience. That is where knowing when and how to reward significant other can become one of the greatest attributes in creating a strong partnership. Women often vocalize when they feel their actions go unappreciated, but little do they know that those same feelings carry over to men as well, who are far less comfortable discussing those emotions.This can cause a lot of tension which may manifest itself in other situations.

Therefore, rewards should always be given for positive behavior. Attention is one of the most powerful things in influencing human thoughts and behaviors - we crave it whether we like to admit it or not. So don't be afraid to pay your partner a compliment on how they washed the dishes or took the dog out or even moved their shoes into the closet. Even if you feel you're being excessive - trust me - you're not! Everyone loves to be praised for their good deeds, and your diligence will help ensure those good deeds become common practice.

I believe it's also important to mention how NOT to reward your loved one. That's to say, when does the reward become punishment? To start, never give someone who is trying to be a genuine help a back-handed compliment. Saying something like, "Oh, you took out the trash? That's a first" is not praise. Despite what you may have heard about these two-sided statements creating more motivation for people to do what you what, it's simply not true. Likewise, always refrain from punishing good intentions, even if they don't turn out the way you want. If your partner decides to mow the lawn, but then doesn't move the bags of leaves to the curb, don't dwell on the one negative proponent of their otherwise very nice gesture. By pointing out what is wrong without properly highlighting what is right you're creating the illusion that this person cannot make you happy, which will give them less drive to do that task in the future. If a task was attempted, but not carried out fully or up to par, still acknowledge the good parts and perhaps make a few suggestions. Or, let it slide for that afternoon, or even until the next day, before mentioning "Hey, did you happen to take the leaves to the curb? No? That's alright, I'll do it, you worked really hard getting the whole lawn done." That's what true communication, respect, and love for one another boils down to.

I encourage everyone, man or woman, married or not, to be on constant surveillance of all the positive things your partner brings to the relationship. Shower them with adoration and affection and let them know they are needed and appreciated. These were just some thoughts I had on this topic! Hope it was worth reading!

With Love, EggHead
